evidence_items.content: Chief complaint: 2 days of left orbital pain
Medical history: hypertension controlled with lisinopril
Medical history: several months of epiphora without prior dacryocystitis
Visual acuity: 20/25 OD and 20/400 OS
Edematous, hyperemic left eyelids
Diffuse limitation in extraocular movements in the left eye
Normal intraocular pressure
Normal fundi on both sides

Initial CT with contrast: Left-sided lacrimal sac abscess with postseptal fat stranding largely limited to the extraconal space, minimal sinus mucosal thickening, and opacification of both nasolacrimal ducts
Follow-up CT: Increased abscess size with globe compression. Minimal intraconal fat stranding, and unremarkable optic nerve appearance
MRI/MRA: Patent ophthalmic artery; diffusion-weighted imaging showed acute injury to the entire orbital segment of the left optic nerve
Initial cultures isolated gram-positive cocci in chains; later identified as pan-susceptible Streptococcus pyogenes

options.description: Orbital abscess secondary to acute dacryocystitis
Acute dacryocystitis with secondary optic nerve injury

evidence_items.content: Chief complaint: multiple bluish, partially keratotic papules and nodules on the lower legs
Age of onset: lesions started growing at age 24
Lesions had been bleeding occasionally after trauma
Patient uses a wheelchair due to right-sided hemiparesis and hemianopsia
Right-sided hemiparesis and hemianopsia caused by an intracranial hemorrhage
Recurrent seizures at age 4
Lipolymphedema of the lower legs attributed to functional venous insufficiency
Family history of similar conditions in the patient's father and aunt
Father died of an intracranial hemorrhage in his early 70s
Sonography demonstrated intradermal slow-flow vascular malformations
Maximum diameter of vascular malformations: 1.2 cm
Histopathology revealed a well-circumscribed lesion with hyperkeratosis and acanthosis
Histopathology revealed dilated venous-like malformations with continuous smooth muscle
Histopathology revealed thrombosis in the upper dermis
Genetic testing detected a heterozygous pathogenic KRIT1 variant

cases.question: What is the most likely diagnosis?
cases.vignette:
A female patient in her early 50s presented with multiple (approximately 10) bluish, partially keratotic papules and nodules on the lower legs. The lesions had been growing very slowly in number and size since age 24 and had been bleeding occasionally after trauma. The patient used a wheelchair due to right-sided hemiparesis and hemianopsia caused by an intracranial hemorrhage. At age 4, she had recurrent seizures. She had lipolymphedema of the lower legs attributed to functional venous insufficiency with insufficient venous pump activity, and had been wearing compression stockings for years. Family history revealed similar conditions in the patient's father and aunt, with the father having died of an intracranial hemorrhage in his early 70s.

Multiple bluish, partially keratotic papules and nodules on the lower legs. Lipolymphedema of the lower legs was present. Right-sided hemiparesis and hemianopsia were noted.

- Sonography: Demonstrated intradermal slow-flow vascular malformations with a maximum diameter of 1.2 cm.

- Histopathology:
  Image Description: Biopsy revealed a well-circumscribed lesion with hyperkeratosis and acanthosis of the epidermis overlying a conglomerate of dilated venous-like malformations with continuous smooth muscle in the upper dermis, partly showing thrombosis.

- Genetic Testing:
  Result: Detection of a heterozygous pathogenic KRIT1 variant.

evidence_items.content: Chief complaint: 2-year history of multiple, slowly growing, infiltrated erythematous-violaceous patches and plaques
Location of patches and plaques: left upper arm to the left side of her chest
No triggers such as local infection, insect bite, or trauma occurred before lesion appearance
No fever, weight loss, or fatigue
Multiple firm, nonscaly, purple erythematous patches and plaques with irregular borders on her left axilla, medial upper arm, and lateral thoracic region
No extracutaneous involvement was observed
Histopathological examination: Thin-walled, irregularly branched blood vessels dispersed between thickened collagen bundles
Endothelial cells were plump but displayed no significant cytologic atypia
Immunohistochemistry results: Positive for CD31, CD34, Ki-67 (<1%)
Immunohistochemistry results: Negative for podoplanin (D2-40), human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8)
Image A: Clinical presentation of multiple nonscaly, erythematous-violaceous patches and plaques with irregular borders on the patient's left axilla, medial upper arm, and lateral thoracic region
Image B: Histopathological examination (hematoxylin-eosin) showing irregularly branched, thin-walled blood vessels dissecting through collagen bundles within the superficial to mid dermis

Image C: Detailed histopathology (hematoxylin-eosin) showing irregularly branched, thin-walled blood vessels with plump endothelial cells dispersed between thickened collagen bundles without signs of atypia
Image D: Immunohistochemistry showing endothelial cells positive for cluster of differentiation (CD) 31

evidence_items.content: Chief complaint: progressive unilateral skin hardening on right thigh and buttock for 7 years
Age: 11 years
Birth history: born to healthy parents
Medical history: no medical disease
Physical examination: ill-defined, stony-hard plaque on right thigh and buttock
Loss of skin elasticity on affected area
Mild hypertrichosis and hyperpigmentation on affected skin
Limited motion of right limb joint
Laboratory tests: normal results for routine blood tests
Laboratory tests: normal results for autoantibodies
Laboratory tests: normal results for immunoglobulins
Laboratory tests: normal results for C-reactive protein
Laboratory tests: normal results for erythrocyte sedimentation rate
Imaging studies: MRI of right thigh demonstrated slight thickening of subcutaneous tissue and T2 signal abnormality
Histopathological findings: normal epidermis and mild pigmentation along the basal layer
Histopathological findings: subtle increase in density of fibroblasts extending to the subcutis and forming adipocyte entrapment
Histopathological findings: no evidence of inflammation
Dense reticular dermis extended below well-preserved appendages
Immunohistochemical staining: increased expression of CD34 in the reticular dermis
Alcian blue staining: negative
MRI of right thigh

cases.question: What is the most likely diagnosis?
cases.vignette:
An 11-year-old boy presented with progressive unilateral skin hardening on his right thigh and buttock for 7 years. Recently, the motion of his right limb joint was slightly limited. He was born to healthy parents and did not have any medical disease.

There was an ill-defined, stony-hard plaque involving his right thigh above the patella extending to his right buttocks with loss of skin elasticity. The affected skin was associated with mild hypertrichosis and hyperpigmentation.

- Laboratory tests: Normal results for routine blood tests, autoantibodies, immunoglobulins, C-reactive protein, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate.- Imaging studies:  Image Title: MRI of right thigh  Image Description: Demonstrated slight thickening of subcutaneous tissue and T2 signal abnormality- Pathological examination:  - Histopathological findings: Normal epidermis and mild pigmentation along the basal layer with subtle increase in density of fibroblasts extending to the subcutis and forming adipocyte entrapment but no evidence of inflammation. Dense reticular dermis extended below well-preserved appendages  - Immunohistochemical staining: Increased expression of CD34 in the reticular dermis  - Alcian blue staining: Negative
